The Setup

To evaluate the limit of sine and cosine as x approaches c, we represent both angles on a unit circle. Point Q is fixed at angle c, and point P is placed at a variable angle x.

plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 1.6.1
plan.contextChunk: This figure shows the unit circle with a fixed angle c and a variable angle x measured from the positive horizontal axis, illustrating the continuity of the sine and cosine functions. Point Q(cos c, sin c) is marked in blue at angle c, and point P(cos x, sin x) is marked in red at angle x; an arrow indicates that P moves toward Q as x approaches c. A caption box at the bottom reads: As x approaches c the point P approaches the point Q. The figure provides a geometric motivation for the limits lim_{x->c} sin x = sin c and lim_{x->c} cos x = cos c, establishing that sin and cos are continuous at every point c.

interactionPlan.concept: The continuity of the sine and cosine functions is geometrically demonstrated by showing that as angle x approaches angle c, the point P(cos x, sin x) merges with Q(cos c, sin c) on the unit circle.
elements: x-axis and y-axis with arrows
Unit circle (solid blue arc on the right half, dashed on the left)
Origin point (0,0)
Point Q (blue dot) at angle c, with label 'Q(cos c, sin c)'
Point P (red dot) at angle x, with label 'P(cos x, sin x)'
Black radius line from origin to Q
Red radius line from origin to P
Purple shaded sector between the two radii
Angle arc for c starting from the positive x-axis, labeled 'c'
Angle arc for x starting from the positive x-axis, labeled 'x'
Curved arrow outside the circle indicating the path from P to Q
Boxed caption text: 'As x approaches c the point P approaches the point Q.'

interactions.label: Target angle c
interactions.teaches: Sets the fixed target point Q on the unit circle to establish the limit we are evaluating.

interactions.label: Variable angle x
interactions.teaches: Manually varying x shows the point P moving along the unit circle, visually demonstrating that its coordinates approach Q's coordinates.

interactions.label: Animate x → c
interactions.teaches: Continuously oscillating x around c confirms the two-sided limit: the gap between P and Q shrinks to zero regardless of the direction of approach.

demo_steps.title: The Setup
demo_steps.narration: To evaluate the limit of sine and cosine as x approaches c, we represent both angles on a unit circle. Point Q is fixed at angle c, and point P is placed at a variable angle x.

demo_steps.title: Approaching from below
demo_steps.narration: As x gets closer to c from below, the point P(cos x, sin x) slides along the circle toward Q. The physical distance between them shrinks to zero.

demo_steps.title: Approaching from above
demo_steps.narration: The exact same geometric convergence happens if x approaches c from above. Because the points merge, their coordinates must also merge, proving that sine and cosine are continuous everywhere.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Because the geometric distance between points P and Q shrinks to zero as angle x approaches angle c, their coordinates (cos x, sin x) and (cos c, sin c) must also continuously converge.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Draw a standard 2D Cartesian coordinate system. Draw a unit circle, centered at the origin, with a solid light-blue stroke on the right half and dashed on the left half. Place a blue dot for Q at angle c (approx 60 degrees) and a red dot for P at angle x (approx 20 degrees). Connect the origin to Q with a black line and to P with a red line. Fill the circular sector between these radii with a radial purple gradient fading toward the origin. Add arcs near the origin denoting angles x and c from the positive x-axis. Add a curved arrow outside the circle pointing from P to Q. Render the caption in a clean rectangular box centered at the bottom.

authoredContext:
Recall from trigonometry that the graphs of sin x and cos x are drawn as continuous curves. We will not formally prove that these functions are continuous, but we can motivate this fact by letting c be a fixed angle in radian measure and x a variable angle in radian measure. If, as illustrated in Figure 1.6.1, the angle x approaches the angle c, then the point P(cos x,sin x) moves along the unit circle toward Q(cos c,sin c), and the coordinates of P approach the
corresponding coordinates of Q. This implies that
lim
x→c
sin x = sin c and limx→c
cos x = cos c (1)
Thus, sin x and cos x are continuous at the arbitrary point c; that is, these functions are continuous everywhere.
